title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design used shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reused the same deterministic validator for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring; these two frozen design choices render the preregistered primary estimand effectively untestable in this execution because identical shared candidates accepted by the deterministic validator produce identical outcomes in both conditions. The preregistered study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory, artifact‑grounded results: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded outcomes, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design produced a deterministic ceiling, and artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can synthesize syntactically plausible configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds, while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in infrastructure‑as‑code and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, and repair/rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes? Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks. Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reusing a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction; and (4) concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations grounded in archived traces.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Representative verified prior work includes intent‑to‑configuration and intent‑driven network configuration studies that demonstrate feasibility of automated translation (Nguyen et al., Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using Large Language Models, 2024); IaC/tool‑augmented verifier training (Jana et al., TerraFormer, 2026) that shows verifier‑guided approaches improve IaC correctness; and deterministic network verification and reachability methods that are effective for offline and emulated checks (ensemble/coverage verification literature). Surveys of agentic LLMs for operations and safety/verification (various 2024–2026 reviews) highlight both potential and failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools) and call for action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility and surface practical design pitfalls. Key verified sources used for grounding and nearest‑work comparison are listed among the cited record identifiers.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). The primary confirmatory estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test was used for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes. Critical preregistered semantics (explicit). Per the preregistration we set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false) so that a single LLM generation per task was delivered identically to baseline and guarded episodes. We also preregistered deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer. Explicitly noting this design choice here: because the same shared candidate was presented to both conditions and the same deterministic validator adjudicated runtime acceptance and post‑hoc scoring, the preregistered primary estimand is effectively untestable for generator×guard closed‑loop effects in this execution—identical accepted candidates necessarily yield identical outcomes in both arms. Adapter semantics and episode flow. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and scorer. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini (one model call per pair), delivered that candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed it to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied deterministic intent‑constraint validation. The preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair_applied flags and validation_before/after states were recorded. Task generation, difficulty metadata, and replay checks. Tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record includes structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; pairs failing replay or encountering simulator errors would be flagged and excluded per the preregistered missingness_plan. Confirmatory analysis procedures. The primary analysis used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05). The exact McNemar test was reported for corroboration. Secondary outcomes included bootstrap CI for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts. All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived.
sections.results: Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded. Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). Contingency counts extracted directly from archived analysis artifacts: baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency: n_11 = 400; n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Preregistered permutation test p = 1.0; exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Repair and rollback observations. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. Diagnostic on difficulty metadata and benchmark diversity. Each task record in execution/task_manifest.jsonl contains a difficulty label; the manifest therefore supports deterministic aggregation by auditors. Representative sample entries included in the archived manifest (first six representative tasks) show one medium, two hard, and three very_hard tasks among that subset. Because the full per‑task labels are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, auditors can reproduce an explicit aggregated difficulty summary directly from that artifact; the manuscript reports the representative sample here and points to the manifest for full aggregated counts. Statistical interpretation. The observed ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference of ≈0.10 with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply.
sections.discussion: Cause of the uninformative primary estimand. Two preregistered design choices together produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings. Consequences for power and inference. The preregistered power calculation relied on within‑pair variability that did not occur. The deterministic ceiling thus invalidates the power rationale and collapses inferential uncertainty: exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the observed data but cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would have improved outcomes under an alternative design that preserved generator variance. Artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening recommendations. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete, preregisterable changes that preserve signal for generator×guard interactions and that can be implemented immediately from the archived artifacts: (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has bona fide opportunities to accept, block, or request repair; (2) use distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to prevent conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; (3) preregister a controlled fraction of perturbation seeds guaranteed to produce nontrivial baseline failure rates (the deterministic task generator supports reproducible adversarial seeding); (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling to guarantee a minimum proportion of very_hard tasks so measurable baseline errors occur (per‑task difficulty labels are archived); and (5) instrument and preregister repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as secondary outcomes (these fields already exist in validator_trace and repair logs). Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners, two practical lessons: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide potential benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve signal for guard interventions by incorporating independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the full preregistration and execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations above provide concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings. Reproducibility note: all execution and analysis artifacts supporting the reported numbers are archived (execution/* and analysis/*). Disclosure Statement: see the mandatory Disclosure Statement below. Final interpretive boundary: the null paired difference observed is a valid artifact‑grounded outcome for the preregistered design and should not be taken as general evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary; instead it illustrates how specific preregistered design choices can eliminate the statistical signal needed to evaluate verifier utility.

Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints were selected pre‑lock by the Research Director and limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. Permitted tools and capabilities: hosted model API calls, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across episodes). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample counts (for the first six representative tasks) and points readers to the manifest for full aggregated counts rather than inventing aggregated totals in the text.
